newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Weak Australian retail raises growth concerns.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Weak Australian retail raises growth concerns.

text.p: A depressed retail sector has left open the possibility that Australia's record run of economic growth may have come to an end, but it did not necessarily increase the chances of a near term rate cut, analysts said.
Anecdotal evidence had suggested that Christmas was not a happy time for retailers, and the hard data backed it up on Tuesday, showing a 1.0 percent fall in December retail trade.
"This confirms the story that both retailers and other business related to the industry have been telling us," National Australia Bank senior economist Tim Pfitzner said.
Market forecasts had centred on a 0.5 percent rise for the month. In trend terms, the series has fallen in each of the last five months, unmatched in the series' 35 year history.

"The closest we came to it was a period in July to September 1992 when there was zero (trend) growth," an ABS spokesman said. More importantly, real retail trade fell 1.3 percent over the December quarter, well under median forecasts of a 0.5 percent fall and the largest quarterly fall since June 1983.
Retail trade accounts for around a quarter of GDP, and the fall in real terms implied a detraction of about 0.3 percentage points from December quarter GDP.
However, as other areas of private consumption included in GDP are expected to be stronger than retail, analysts expected overall private consumption would be close to flat.

"If this is realised and the long awaited stock run-down occurred in the December quarter, the current run of 21 consecutive quarters of continuous economic growth could end," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary.
That run of 21 quarters is a recorded unmatched since the quarterly GDP series began. However, despite the weaker data, negative GDP was far from a foregone conclusion.

Merrill lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas noted that in last week's mid year budget review, the government changed the underlying composition of the 3.5 percent growth forecast for 1996/97 (July-June), winding back consumption forecasts and lifting business investment forecasts.
On the monthly data, analysts said while the December data suggested a weak economy, January figures, due on March 4, were needed before a full interpretation of the data could be made.
This is because there appears to have been a change in consmer spending patterns over recent years that the seasonal adjustment process has not yet caught up with.
Conusmers were delaying purchases until the post-Christmas/New Year sales, in effect moving spending into January. For that reason the large fall in December may be reversed next month.
"The numbers suggest that, obviously, the consumer cut back spending ... but because of the change in spending patterns, I wouldn't read too much into this," Douglas said.
Partly for that reason, analysts said that while a rate cut was still well and truly on the cards, it would not automatically follow on from the weaker than expected data.

Apart from the doubts over the seasonal adjustment, there had no been enough time to judge the impact of the rate cuts in November and December. And while retail remained depressed, there were some signs of recovery in other areas, such as housing, that suggested the economy was beginning to strengthen.
Finally, the Reserve Bank was expected to wait until it had received updated wages data to assess the inflation outlook, including the outcome of the unions' "living wage" case.
"All these considerations favour a 'wait and see' approach by the monetary authorities in the near term," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Bylthe said.
"Nevertheless the bias over the next few months clearly remains on the side of a further easing," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
